verdicts.note: Otys and Ephialtes (the Aloadae) were twin brothers, so 'the two brothers' is accurate. It keeps Jowett's reference and no longer collides with 'as they had once done to the giants' two sentences later, which is a separate story (the Giants blasted with thunderbolts). Homer's 'dared to climb up to heaven' still identifies them. No new invention.

The choice is sound. Plato 190b reads 'hoti kai he selene amphoteron metechei': the moon 'partakes of both', the same verb used for the man-woman, who 'partakes of both' sexes. Jowett's loose 'made up of' allows this reading. It comes from the Greek, not from another translation (BL2 reached the same plain phrase without seeing any source). 'Shares in both' also brings out the parallel with the double-natured man-woman. It is weaker than 'made up of' only in a mythic aside, not in an argument step, and it reads naturally aloud.

Sound. Jowett's 'in obedience to the law' renders 192b 'hypo tou nomou anankazontai', and nomos covers both law and custom. The doublet keeps Jowett's 'law', unpacks the shifted sense in two words, and keeps the compulsion ('require'). It adds no fact, and the argument is unchanged: by nature they are not inclined to marry, and they do so only under compulsion. It does not import a single-sense reading such as 'custom' alone, and it reads naturally.

Now faithful to Jowett ('as the Arcadians were dispersed into villages by the Lacedaemonians'). The invented and imprecise 'city of the Arcadians' is gone. The repeated 'dispersed' ('the god has dispersed us, just as ... dispersed the Arcadians') mirrors Plato's single verb dioikizo, so the comparison lands clearly by ear. Optional, and older than this round: BL2 heard 'the Lacedaemonians, the Spartans' as possibly two peoples. The appositive matches the book's 7.60 gloss, so it does not block this edit.

Right in direction. 'Did I not know', 'I should be' and 'But, for all that, I am not without hopes' are gone, and every element of Jowett is kept ('nothing left to say' is implied by 'after ... said already'). But the recast keeps Jowett's Victorian idiom 'after the world of things that have been said already' ('a world of' = a vast number of). That phrase is inside the very sentence BL2 quoted as 'the first abrupt drop into Victorian English'. Aloud, 'the world of things' can also be heard in its physical-world sense until the relative clause arrives. Replacing only that phrase with 'the vast number of things' keeps Jowett's hyperbole (Plato: 'polla kai pantodapa', many and varied things) and Eryximachus's slightly grand register. Everything else is the editor's wording, unchanged.
verdicts.proposed_replace: 'Indeed, I am not going to attack you,' said Eryximachus, 'for I thought your speech charming. If I did not know that Agathon and Socrates are masters in the art of love, I would be really afraid that they would have nothing left to say, after the vast number of things that have been said already. But even so, I have hopes.'

verdicts.note: Faithful and much easier by ear. 'Lose my nerve' = 'disconcerted' (thorubetho, flustered). 'The audience has been led to expect' keeps Jowett's 'expectation raised', whose implied agent is Socrates. It also sets up 'rattle your nerves' in 5.11. Voice and quotes are fine.

Nothing is lost. Element by element: 'strangely forgetful' kept; vocative 'Agathon' kept; 'if I thought' becomes 'to think'; 'your nerves could be fluttered' becomes 'could rattle your nerves'; 'at a small party of friends' kept (Greek 'heneka hemon oligon anthropon', on account of us few people, even closer); 'courage and magnanimity' becomes 'courage and greatness of spirit' (megalophrosune); 'when your own compositions were about to be exhibited' becomes 'when your own plays were about to be performed' ('plays' is an accurate unpacking, since Agathon's compositions are tragedies, and it supports later chapters that assume he is a playwright); 'came upon the stage with the actors' kept ('came up onto', matching anabainontos epi ton okribanta); 'faced the vast theatre' becomes 'faced that vast theater'; 'altogether undismayed' becomes 'without the least dismay'. 'I remember' is only the positive restatement of 'forgetful of', and the Greek 'idon' (having seen) supports it, so no fact or motive is added. The vast-theater / small-party contrast survives. Ending on the theater leads straight into Agathon's 'my head is so full of the theater' (5.12). Socrates' ironic flattery is intact, and the quotes balance.

Faithful. 'How much more a man of sense fears a few good judges than a crowd of fools' = Jowett's 'how much more formidable to a man of sense a few good judges are than many fools' (Plato 'phoberoteroi'). 'Crowd' for 'many' suits the theater context. A contraction is fine for Agathon in conversation.

Restores Jowett's 'attributing' and 'want of refinement' (Plato 'agroikon': boorish, unrefined) in place of the sharper 'accuse ... of' and the aesthetic 'lack of taste'. It is faithful and reads acceptably. Optional polish only: 'I would be very wrong, Agathon, to attribute that or any other lack of refinement to you' would stop an unstressed 'that' after 'attribute to you, Agathon,' from sounding for a moment like the start of a clause. This is not required.

'In their presence' was Jowett's own redundant clarifier. Plato 194c has only 'ton de pollon ouk an aischunoio ei ti oioio aischron poiein'. 'In front of the many' carries the sense, so nothing is lost. It now parallels 5.13's 'in front of him', which makes Socrates' half-finished trap easier to hear.

It follows the glossary exactly: the term is named once, at its first use. In the successor, 1.46's 'encomiast' is rendered 'a single poet to praise him', so 5.16 is the first 'encomium'. The spaced em dashes replace the glossary's parentheses under the no-brackets rule. 'What we call' sits naturally in Phaedrus's mouth, and later passages can simply say 'speech of praise'.

Jowett's 'which I ought to receive from him and from every one' means what is due to Phaedrus. 'Which he and everyone else owe me' is the modern equivalent. It fits the dialogue's framing: in ch. 1 Eryximachus offers the speeches to Phaedrus as 'a contribution' (Greek eranos, a share each member owes). The debt image also runs on into the next sentence, 'paid your tribute to the god'. It fixes BL2's 'receive' problem and keeps Phaedrus earnest. If the lead prefers the duty sense of Plato's 'anankaion ... moi ... apodexasthai' ('I must receive'), 'which I have to collect from him and from everyone else' would also work, but it is not needed.

A correct mechanical fix. It removes the last unspaced Victorian ':—' in these chapters and matches 6.12's 'as follows:' and 6.0's closing 'tender:'. The colon before the closing quote properly hands over to Agathon's speech, which the edition sets unquoted from 6.0 onward (a pre-existing, book-wide choice).

Faithful and plainer: 'no reason not to go on', 'since', 'many other chances to talk with Socrates'. Keeping 'shall' is acceptable for Agathon's slightly formal register. The order 'first say how I ought to speak, and then speak' is kept, and 6.0 then does exactly that (the right way to praise first).

The glosses are accurate. Hesiod is the poet of the Theogony. Parmenides wrote his philosophy as a hexameter poem, so 'philosopher-poet' is more exact than BL2's 'philosopher'. Both are identical to the successor's 2.0 ('As the poet Hesiod says') and 2.2 ('the philosopher-poet Parmenides'). Repeating them here is justified after the long gap since ch. 2. The sentence is now long (the subject sits about 20 words before 'were'), but each segment is short and it parses aloud. No change needed.

Accurate. Necessity (Ananke) is the personified power of constraint, and 'the power of compulsion' defines the word without adding a mythic claim. The four words are within the gloss allowance. They prepare 'ruled by Necessity' in 6.4 and sharpen Agathon's contrast in 6.3, where force never comes near Love and all serve him of their own free will. Plato 195c: 'Anankei kai ouk Eroti gegonenai' (came about through Necessity and not through Love).

Restores Jowett's 'he can neither do nor suffer wrong'. For the record: Plato 196b is plain indicative ('oute adikei oute adikeitai', neither wrongs nor is wronged), so the modal is Jowett's own emphasis, not a reading taken from elsewhere. Jowett is the baseline, and Agathon's reasons that follow (force never comes near him; everyone serves him willingly) support the modal. The parallel 'can neither do ... nor suffer ...' is grammatical and reads cleanly.

Jowett's own words. Plato 197a 'phanos' / 'skoteinos' (bright / dark) confirms the light-darkness antithesis. Next to 'comes into the light of fame', 'walks in darkness' is heard as obscurity, not moral darkness. It keeps Agathon's ornament.

'Brings them together' = 'makes them to meet together' (Plato 'xunodous ... titheis xunienai', making them come together in such gatherings). Only the archaic causative is removed. The deliberate jingles around it are untouched.

'Song' matches Plato's 'oides ... hen aidei' (the song he sings) better than Victorian 'strain'. It keeps Jowett's 'sweetly singing ... sweet' doubling. No echo is lost: the successor's 6.10 already renders Socrates' 'Farewell then to such a strain' as 'goodbye to that style of praise'.

Both the naming and the signpost are right. 'Told Socrates' makes Jowett's 'him' explicit. 'Socrates added' removes the misreading BL2 found: after 'Aristodemus said', a bare 'he' is heard as Aristodemus. 'Added' is Jowett's verb and correct, since Socrates resumes after the company's reply to his question in 6.10. 'Told' for 'bid' matches keleuein. 'So that I can build my argument on the points he agrees to' = 'in order that I may take his admissions as the premisses of my discourse' (Plato 'anomologesamenos'). It states chapter 7's method in plain words. Nothing is dropped, and the quotes balance.

Plain, faithful equivalents: 'You have my permission' / 'Ask your questions' for 'I grant the permission' / 'put your questions'. 'Went on' fits Jowett's 'proceeded' (Socrates is already speaking). The closing colon matches 5.17.

summary: 22 round-2 edits in 17 paragraphs (5.1-6.12) checked against Jowett (pg1600), with Plato's Greek where an edit chooses a reading. Result: 21 accept, 1 revise, 0 reject. Revise: R2-89 (5.8). The recast is right, but it keeps Jowett's idiom 'after the world of things that have been said already', which sits in the very sentence BL2 flagged as Victorian. Proposed: 'the vast number of things'; nothing else changes. Priority items: 5.11 recast keeps every element of Jowett (see R2-91 note); 'I remember' only restates 'forgetful of'. 5.4 'law and custom' is a sound two-word unpacking of nomos. 5.1 'shares in both' is Plato's 'metechei' and within Jowett's 'made up of'. 6.0 glosses are accurate and match 2.0 and 2.2. 6.3 'can' restores Jowett (Plato's Greek is plain indicative, so the modal is Jowett's emphasis; the baseline governs). 5.16 names 'encomium' once, at its first use, per the glossary. 6.11 'Socrates added' fixes the Aristodemus ambiguity. Whole paragraphs: all 17 AFTER texts were read in full. No new problems: no broken sentences; quotes balance (5.1, 5.4 and 5.5 correctly stay open for Aristophanes' continuing speech, and 5.1's nested double quote continues into 5.2); straight quotes, spaced em dashes, American spelling, no ellipses. Optional polish, not required: 5.13 word order (R2-61 note); 5.16 'collect' as an alternative to 'owe me' (R2-94 note); 5.5 'the Lacedaemonians, the Spartans' (pre-existing). Pre-existing and untouched by round 2: Agathon's speech (6.0-6.6) is unquoted. F2 already raised this as a book-wide decision.
